name: Reuters Institute: Research on AI in News and Journalism
title: Reuters Institute: Research on AI in News and Journalism
answer: The Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at Oxford publishes survey research on how audiences and journalists use and regard generative AI in news. Its most useful single finding is that weekly AI use for news remains low, rising from 3% to 6% across six countries, even as general generative AI use jumped from 40% to 61%, which shows a widening gap between everyday AI adoption and news consumption.

sections.body: The Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at the University of Oxford publishes this body of survey research, reports and commentary on artificial intelligence in news. The material spans a 2024 Digital News Report chapter on public attitudes, a 2025 generative AI and news report, a survey of 1,004 UK journalists conducted between August and November 2024, a six-country public opinion study, a conference summary from 26 March, and a hub page collecting research, reporting and programmes on AI and the future of news. The Institute states it has worked with journalists, editors and technologists since 2016 to understand what AI might mean for news.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Across six countries, Argentina, Denmark, France, Japan, the UK and the USA, the share who have ever used a standalone generative AI system such as ChatGPT rose from 40% to 61%, and weekly use nearly doubled from 18% to 34%. ChatGPT is the most popular system at 22% weekly usage. Information seeking has become the primary use case, more than doubling to 24% weekly, while news consumption remains limited at 6%, up from 3%. Among AI-for-news users, latest news and help summarising, evaluating or rewriting are most common. Awareness of AI tools rose from 78% to 90%. Trust in ChatGPT averages 29%, ahead of Gemini at 18%, Copilot at 12% and Meta AI at 12%. In the UK journalist survey, 56% use AI professionally at least weekly, mostly for transcription, translation and copy-editing, while 62% see AI as a large threat to journalism and only 15% see it as a large opportunity. The Digital News Report 2024 chapter found only 36% are comfortable with news made by humans with AI help and 19% with news made mostly by AI.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source gives many specific figures. Ever-use of generative AI rose from 40% to 61% and weekly use from 18% to 34% across six countries. Weekly AI news use rose from 3% to 6%. ChatGPT weekly usage is 22%, and trust in it averages 29% against 18% for Gemini, 12% for Copilot and 12% for Meta AI. Among UK journalists, 56% use AI professionally at least weekly, 49% for transcription at least monthly, 62% see AI as a large threat and 15% as a large opportunity. In the 2024 chapter, 45% had heard a large or moderate amount about AI, 36% were comfortable with human-led AI news and 19% with mostly AI news.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in media would use this source for measured, survey-based evidence on both sides of the newsroom door. It quantifies audience behaviour, showing that general AI adoption is rising fast while news use stays marginal, and it documents journalists' own adoption patterns and anxieties. The findings on trust, comfort and the gap between optimists for entertainment and pessimists for news give a grounded basis for judging claims about AI transforming journalism, and the hub page points to further work on chatbots, crawlers, licensing and personalisation.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Media

sections.body: The material is survey-based and largely covers six countries, with the journalist survey limited to the UK, so it is not a global census. Several items are summaries or hub listings rather than full reports, and the hub page notes that applications for its 2026 programme are closed. The research describes attitudes and self-reported use rather than measured newsroom outcomes, and the qualitative work rests on 45 participants in three countries.
